author: A Robot
objectives: Students will identify the structural components of DNA — the sugar-phosphate backbone, nitrogenous bases, and hydrogen bonds — and how they assemble into a double helix.
Students will apply complementary base-pairing rules (A-T, G-C) and explain why these pairings occur.
Students will describe the antiparallel orientation of DNA strands and how 5'-to-3' directionality determines it.
Students will trace the roles of helicase, SSBs, DNA polymerase, and DNA ligase at the replication fork.
Students will explain leading vs lagging strand synthesis and Okazaki fragments due to the unidirectional activity of DNA polymerase.
Students will articulate the semiconservative nature of replication and predict daughter molecule compositions.

modules.description: An introduction to the schematic ladder representation of DNA, highlighting the sugar-phosphate backbone and nitrogenous bases.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Identify the structural components of DNA — the sugar-phosphate backbone and the four nitrogenous bases.
Recognize the regular repeating structure of DNA before introducing 3D geometry.

clips.changeMeaning: Initial setup showing the schematic ladder.
clips.narration: Welcome to the molecular biology lab. Before us is a schematic ladder representation of DNA. The vertical lines represent the sugar-phosphate backbones, while the horizontal rungs are the base pairs.

clips.changeMeaning: Highlight the specific base pairing colors.
clips.narration: Each rung is composed of two bases meeting in the middle. Notice the color coding: adenine in red always pairs with thymine in blue, and guanine in yellow always pairs with cytosine in green.

modules.description: Transitioning from the schematic ladder to the realistic 3D double helix.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Describe how the structural components assemble into the double helix.
Map the schematic representation to the realistic 3D geometry.

clips.changeMeaning: Initial state showing the ladder again.
clips.narration: While the ladder schematic is useful, real DNA in cells is a three-dimensional structure. Let's see what happens when this ladder twists.

clips.changeMeaning: Hide the ladder and show the realistic double helix.
clips.narration: The ladder twists into the familiar double-helix shape. The backbones spiral around a common axis, and the base pairs stack along the interior. It completes one full turn approximately every ten base pairs.

clips.changeMeaning: Add rotation to let students observe the grooves.
clips.narration: You can observe the major and minor grooves in the geometry. Feel free to toggle back and forth between the schematic and the helix to build your mental map.

modules.description: Exploring the antiparallel orientation and 5'-to-3' directionality of DNA strands.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Describe the antiparallel orientation of the two strands of DNA.
Explain how the 5'-to-3' directionality of the sugar-phosphate backbone determines this arrangement.

clips.changeMeaning: Show arrows indicating the directionality of the strands.
clips.narration: Let's examine the ends of the DNA strands. You'll notice arrows indicating direction: one strand points up, the other points down.

clips.changeMeaning: Highlight the 5' and 3' labels.
clips.narration: These arrows represent the 5-prime to 3-prime directionality. These labels refer to specific carbon atoms of the sugar ring at the ends of each backbone.

clips.changeMeaning: Rotate to show it is a fixed chemical property.
clips.narration: The two strands always run in opposite directions. This antiparallel arrangement is not optional — it is forced by the directional chemistry of the sugar-phosphate backbone.

modules.description: Interactive base-pairing activity to reinforce complementary rules.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Apply complementary base-pairing rules (A with T, G with C).
Explain the relationship between specific pairings and the number of hydrogen bonds.

clips.changeMeaning: Introduce the template strand and loose bases.
clips.narration: Here we have a partial ladder structure. The strand on the left is complete, but the one on the right is missing its bases. Below are loose bases you can drag into place.

clips.changeMeaning: Simulate pairing an Adenine to a Thymine.
clips.narration: When an Adenine is placed across from a Thymine, it snaps into place forming two hydrogen bonds.

clips.changeMeaning: Simulate pairing a Guanine to a Cytosine.
clips.narration: Similarly, a Guanine placed across from a Cytosine forms three hydrogen bonds. This specific pairing is crucial for the strength and accurate copying of DNA.

modules.description: Introducing helicase and the unwinding of the double helix.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Trace the action of helicase at the replication fork.
Identify helicase's function in breaking hydrogen bonds.

clips.changeMeaning: Show helicase positioned at the start of the helix.
clips.narration: Now let's look at DNA replication. The first enzyme involved is helicase, positioned here at one end of the double helix.

clips.changeMeaning: Move helicase to show unwinding.
clips.narration: Helicase moves along the DNA, breaking the hydrogen bonds between base pairs. This unwinds the double helix and exposes the strands so they can be used as templates.

modules.description: The role of single-strand binding proteins in stabilizing the replication fork.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Trace the action of single-strand binding proteins.
Identify the function of SSBs in preventing the strands from re-pairing.

clips.changeMeaning: Show the open, unstable strands.
clips.narration: Behind helicase, the two strands are separated. However, single strands of DNA are unstable and tend to re-pair or fold back on themselves.

clips.changeMeaning: SSBs appear and attach to the strands.
clips.narration: To prevent this, single-strand binding proteins, or SSBs, attach to each exposed strand. They hold the strands open and accessible so replication can proceed.

modules.description: Continuous synthesis of the leading strand by DNA polymerase.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Trace the action of DNA polymerase.
Explain why the leading strand is synthesized continuously due to 5'-to-3' activity.

clips.changeMeaning: Introduce DNA polymerase on the leading strand template.
clips.narration: Next, DNA polymerase binds to an exposed template strand. It can only build a new strand by adding nucleotides to a 3-prime end, meaning it travels 3-prime to 5-prime on the template.

clips.changeMeaning: Move polymerase to synthesize the leading strand continuously.
clips.narration: On this strand, oriented favorably, the polymerase moves continuously, following the replication fork. This creates the continuous leading strand.

modules.description: Discontinuous synthesis of the lagging strand and the role of DNA ligase.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Trace the action of DNA polymerase on the lagging strand and DNA ligase.
Explain why the lagging strand is synthesized discontinuously as Okazaki fragments.

clips.changeMeaning: Introduce the lagging strand problem.
clips.narration: On the other template strand, the 3-prime end points away from the fork. Polymerase cannot follow the fork continuously here.

clips.changeMeaning: Show the formation of Okazaki fragments.
clips.narration: Instead, polymerase works backward in short bursts away from the fork, jumps back, and repeats. This produces short pieces called Okazaki fragments.

clips.changeMeaning: Introduce DNA ligase joining the fragments.
clips.narration: Finally, an enzyme called DNA ligase comes in and joins these Okazaki fragments together into a single continuous strand.

modules.description: An overview of all enzymes working together at the replication fork.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Relate the asymmetry of the replication fork to the unidirectional activity of DNA polymerase on antiparallel templates.

clips.changeMeaning: Show the complete functioning fork.
clips.narration: Here is the completed replication fork in action: helicase at the front unwinding, SSBs holding strands open, leading polymerase moving continuously, lagging polymerase working in fragments, and ligase sealing them.

clips.changeMeaning: Rotate the complex to emphasize the asymmetrical setup forced by the antiparallel structure.
clips.narration: This entire asymmetrical machine is a direct result of the antiparallel structure of DNA we saw earlier. Because polymerase only works in one direction, the two oppositely oriented strands must be copied differently.

modules.description: Exploring the semiconservative nature of DNA replication and predicting outcomes across generations.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Articulate why DNA replication is described as semiconservative.
Predict the composition of daughter molecules after multiple rounds of replication.

clips.changeMeaning: Show the original gold parental DNA.
clips.narration: Let's look at the result of replication. Here is a parental DNA molecule, colored gold to mark the original material.

clips.changeMeaning: Show the first generation of hybrid daughters.
clips.narration: After one round of replication, we have two daughter molecules. Notice they are hybrids: one gold parental strand and one silver newly synthesized strand. This is why replication is called 'semiconservative'.

clips.changeMeaning: Ask the user to predict generation 2.
clips.narration: If these two molecules undergo a second round of replication in a completely silver environment, what will the four resulting molecules look like? Make your prediction.

clips.changeMeaning: Show the four molecules of the second generation.
clips.narration: In the second round, the gold strands are conserved again, creating two hybrid molecules. The silver strands act as templates for new silver strands, creating two fully silver molecules.

modules.description: A comprehensive review of the structural and functional concepts covered in the lab.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Review and consolidate all learning objectives regarding DNA structure and replication.

clips.changeMeaning: Show the recap summary for DNA structure.
clips.narration: To review: we examined the double-helix structure with its sugar-phosphate backbones, the complementary base-pairing rules driven by hydrogen bonds, and the antiparallel 5-prime to 3-prime arrangement of the two strands.

clips.changeMeaning: Show the recap summary for replication.
clips.narration: We also traced the replication fork: helicase unwinds, SSBs stabilize, and DNA polymerase synthesizes a continuous leading strand and a fragmented lagging strand, which ligase then seals. All conserving one parent strand in a semiconservative process.
